routes.description: Establish Christianity through a cumulative public-evidence case in which historically grounded testimony and its theological setting support Jesus's bodily resurrection, while biblical teaching remains compatible with divine goodness and authority.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available historical evidence makes bodily resurrection the best explanation, the surrounding theological context connects that event to Jesus's identity and Christian claims, and the principal reliability and moral-authority objections can be reconciled with Christianity.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative resurrection, identity, reliability, and moral-authority case to the conclusion that Christianity is true and warrants rational commitment.

centralBridges.description: Establish historically grounded resurrection appearances and related facts for which bodily resurrection is the best cumulative explanation.
Establish that the Gospel and apostolic materials are sufficiently early, interlocking, and reliable to support the historical premises.
Show that Jesus's scriptural and theological setting raises the resurrection hypothesis's credibility and connects resurrection to his identity and authority.
Reconcile challenged biblical laws, narratives, and doctrines with the goodness and moral authority attributed to the Christian God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply an evidential framework under which sufficiently strong evidence can overcome a low prior probability for a supernatural explanation.
Explain Christian faith as trust grounded in evidence and prior reasons rather than belief adopted independently of evidence.

routes.description: Withhold acceptance of Christianity by challenging the adequacy and independence of its resurrection sources, denying the inference from resurrection to the wider religion, and presenting biblical teaching and Christian doctrine as incompatible with credible moral authority.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the resurrection case does not meet its required evidential burden, if resurrection would not establish Christianity's further identity and authority claims, or if independent moral objections defeat the claimed authority or warranted allegiance of Christianity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the historical, theological, and moral premises offered do not jointly establish Christianity as true or authoritative.

centralBridges.description: Show that late, disputed, internally divergent, or literarily shaped sources are insufficient to establish an extraordinary bodily resurrection.
Demonstrate that even a resurrection would not by itself establish Jesus's divinity, moral authority, Christian doctrine, or a duty of allegiance.
Show that challenged biblical laws, narratives, and doctrines conflict with the perfect goodness required for divine moral authority.
Challenge prophecy and theological context as independent grounds for raising the prior credibility of Jesus's resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Challenge whether the evidence about apostolic suffering and death establishes sincere, recantable testimony to bodily resurrection.
Require an account of morally significant animal suffering that is compatible with the agency and goodness of the Christian God.

sections.title: Resurrection Appearances and Competing Historical Explanations
sections.rationale: The existence, character, and sincerity of reported appearances supply the principal historical basis for resurrection, while the evidential threshold and availability of non-resurrection explanations determine whether that basis can bear the central historical burden.

sections.title: Gospel Reliability, Corroboration, and Narrative Construction
sections.rationale: The resurrection inference depends on whether Gospel and apostolic materials function as historically grounded testimony; alleged contradictions, literary parallels, interlocking details, and inductive reliability therefore form a distinct source-level clash.

sections.title: Prior Probability, Prophecy, and the Bridge to Christianity
sections.rationale: This issue governs both whether a supernatural resurrection can become credible in Jesus's theological setting and whether such an event would establish divinity, doctrinal truth, moral authority, or warranted allegiance to Christianity.

sections.title: Biblical Teaching, Atonement, and Divine Moral Authority
sections.rationale: Biblical slavery texts, conquest narratives, salvation and atonement doctrines, and the basis of divine-command morality provide an independent motion-level test of whether Christianity can credibly claim a perfectly good and authoritative source.

sections.title: Suffering, Evidence, and Rational Christian Commitment
sections.rationale: Animal suffering tests the compatibility of Christian theism with divine goodness, while disputes about faith, evidential responsibility, and conditional importance address what would rationally support further inquiry or commitment.
